preamble.whatYouWillLearn: You will reflect points and shapes in horizontal, vertical and diagonal mirror lines and work out the coordinates of the image. You will rotate shapes 90° clockwise or anticlockwise about one of their corners. You will also find the order of rotational symmetry of shapes, letters and patterns, and tell reflections, rotations and translations apart.
preamble.whyItMatters: Reflections and rotations help you picture how shapes move and fit together. Designers, engineers and game makers use them every day, and they are the start of transformation geometry in secondary school.
realWorld: Batik and songket patterns often repeat a motif by reflecting or rotating it
Seeing your reflection in a mirror or a still lake at Putrajaya
A ceiling fan or a car wheel has rotational symmetry
Turning a puzzle piece or a block a quarter turn so it fits in a game
Logos and tiles are designed with lines of symmetry so they look balanced

subtopics.title: Reflection in vertical and horizontal lines
subtopics.summary: Reflect points and shapes in the x-axis, the y-axis and lines such as x = 2 or y = 4. Each point ends up the same distance from the mirror line, on the other side.

subtopics.title: Reflection in a diagonal line
subtopics.summary: Reflect points in the diagonal line through (0, 0), (1, 1) and (2, 2), where the coordinates swap places. Stretch: the other diagonal, through (1, -1).

subtopics.title: Rotation about a vertex
subtopics.summary: Rotate shapes a quarter turn (90°) clockwise or anticlockwise about one of their corners and find the image coordinates.

subtopics.title: Symmetry and comparing transformations
subtopics.summary: Find lines of symmetry and the order of rotational symmetry of patterns, complete symmetrical shapes, and tell reflection, rotation and translation apart.

subtopics.title: Rotational symmetry
subtopics.summary: How many times a shape, letter or pattern fits onto itself in one full turn (order 1 to 4).

questions.prompt: Point P is plotted on the grid. It is reflected in the y-axis, shown as the dashed mirror line. What are the coordinates of its image?
questions.solution: The y-axis is a vertical mirror. P(3, 2) is 3 squares to the right of it, so the image is 3 squares to the LEFT, at the same height. Image = (-3, 2).

misconceptions.0: This is a reflection in the x-axis (the horizontal axis). The y-axis is the vertical axis, so the point flips from right to left and only x changes.
misconceptions.1: Only one coordinate changes in a reflection in an axis. Reflecting in the y-axis changes the sign of x; y stays the same.
misconceptions.3: Swapping the numbers is what happens with the diagonal mirror line, not with the y-axis.

questions.skill: reflecting in the x-axis or y-axis

questions.prompt: Point P is plotted on the grid. It is reflected in the x-axis, shown as the dashed mirror line. What are the coordinates of its image?
questions.solution: The x-axis is a horizontal mirror. P(4, -5) is 5 squares below it, so the image is 5 squares ABOVE it, directly over the point. Image = (4, 5).

misconceptions.1: This is a reflection in the y-axis. The x-axis is horizontal, so the point flips from below to above and only y changes.
misconceptions.2: Both signs have changed. A reflection in the x-axis only changes the sign of the y-coordinate.
misconceptions.3: The numbers have been swapped as well. In a reflection in the x-axis, x stays as 4.

questions.skill: reflecting in the x-axis or y-axis

questions.prompt: True or false: When you reflect a point in the x-axis, its y-coordinate stays the same.
questions.solution: The x-axis is a horizontal mirror, so the point flips up or down. That changes the y-coordinate (it changes sign: 3 becomes -3). It is the x-coordinate that stays the same. False.

misconceptions.common: Thinking 'x-axis' means the y-coordinate is left alone. Picture the mirror: a horizontal mirror flips things up and down, so y changes.

questions.skill: reflecting in the x-axis or y-axis

questions.prompt: Point P is plotted on the grid. It is reflected in the mirror line x = 2 shown. What are the coordinates of its image?
questions.solution: The mirror is the vertical line x = 2. P is at x = 5, which is 5 - 2 = 3 squares to the right of the mirror. The image is 3 squares to the left of the mirror: x = 2 - 3 = -1. y does not change. Image = (-1, 3).

misconceptions.0: This reflects in the y-axis (x = 0). The mirror here is the line x = 2, so measure the distance from that line instead.
misconceptions.1: This reflects in a horizontal line y = 2. The line x = 2 is vertical, so the point moves left, not down.
misconceptions.2: The point is 3 units from the mirror, but the image must be 3 units on the OTHER side of the mirror line (2 - 3 = -1), not 3 units from the origin.

questions.skill: reflecting in a vertical or horizontal line

questions.prompt: Point P is plotted on the grid. It is reflected in the mirror line y = 4 shown. What are the coordinates of its image?
questions.solution: The mirror is the horizontal line y = 4. P is at y = 7, which is 7 - 4 = 3 squares above the mirror. The image is 3 squares below the mirror: y = 4 - 3 = 1. x does not change. Image = (1, 1).

misconceptions.0: This reflects in the x-axis (y = 0). The mirror is the line y = 4, so measure from that line.
misconceptions.2: 3 is the DISTANCE from the point to the mirror. The image is 3 units below the mirror line: 4 - 3 = 1.
misconceptions.3: This reflects in the y-axis. A horizontal mirror line moves the point up or down, so x stays as 1.

questions.skill: reflecting in a vertical or horizontal line

questions.prompt: Point P is plotted on the grid. It is reflected in the mirror line y = 1 shown. What is the y-coordinate of the image?
questions.solution: P is at y = 6, which is 6 - 1 = 5 squares above the mirror line y = 1. The image is 5 squares below it: 1 - 5 = -4. The image is (-2, -4), so the y-coordinate is -4.

misconceptions.common: Answering -6 by reflecting in the x-axis instead of the line y = 1, or answering 4 by forgetting that 1 - 5 goes below zero.

questions.skill: reflecting in a vertical or horizontal line

questions.prompt: The grid shows the vertical mirror line x = 3. Select ALL the points that stay in exactly the same place when they are reflected in this mirror line.
questions.solution: A point stays still only if it is ON the mirror line. Every point on the line x = 3 has x-coordinate 3: (3, 0), (3, -5) and (3, 3). The y-coordinate can be anything.

misconceptions.2: (0, 3) has y = 3, not x = 3. It is 3 units left of the mirror, so its image is (6, 3).
misconceptions.4: (-3, 3) is 6 units left of the mirror line x = 3, so it moves to (9, 3).
misconceptions.5: (6, 3) is 3 units right of the mirror line, so it moves to (0, 3).

questions.skill: reflecting in a vertical or horizontal line

questions.prompt: Triangle ABC is drawn on the grid. It is reflected in the x-axis, shown as the dashed mirror line. Which list gives the corners of the image, A', B' and C'?
questions.solution: Read the corners from the grid: A(1, 2), B(4, 2), C(4, 5). Reflecting in the x-axis: keep each x-coordinate and change the sign of each y-coordinate. A(1, 2) to (1, -2), B(4, 2) to (4, -2), C(4, 5) to (4, -5).

misconceptions.0: This is a reflection in the y-axis. Reflecting in the x-axis keeps x the same and changes the sign of y.
misconceptions.2: Every corner must be reflected. C(4, 5) also moves, to (4, -5).
misconceptions.3: The coordinates have been swapped round as well as changing sign. Keep x first and only change the sign of y.

questions.skill: reflecting in the x-axis or y-axis

questions.prompt: True or false: Reflecting the point (2, 5) in the horizontal mirror line y = 5 leaves it in the same place.
questions.solution: The point (2, 5) has y = 5, so it lies ON the mirror line y = 5. Its distance from the mirror is 0, so its image is itself. True.

misconceptions.common: Thinking every point must move in a reflection. Points on the mirror line stay where they are.

questions.skill: reflecting in a vertical or horizontal line

questions.prompt: Point P is reflected in the mirror line x = -1 shown on the grid. Its image, P', is plotted. What are the coordinates of P?
questions.solution: Reflecting back gives the original point. P'(2, 4) is 2 - (-1) = 3 squares right of the mirror line x = -1. So P is 3 squares left of the mirror: x = -1 - 3 = -4. y stays 4. P = (-4, 4).

misconceptions.1: This reflects in the y-axis (x = 0). The mirror line is x = -1, one unit to the left of the y-axis.
misconceptions.2: This reflects in the horizontal line y = -1. The line x = -1 is vertical, so only x changes.
misconceptions.3: The image is 3 units from the mirror (from 2 back to -1). P must be 3 units on the other side of the MIRROR LINE: -1 - 3 = -4, not 3 units from the origin.

questions.skill: reflecting in a vertical or horizontal line

questions.prompt: Point P is reflected in a vertical mirror line. P and its image P' are plotted on the grid. The mirror line is x = ?. Give the missing number.
questions.solution: The mirror line is exactly halfway between a point and its image. Halfway between x = 1 and x = 7 is (1 + 7) / 2 = 4. So the mirror line is x = 4. Check: P(1, 3) is 3 squares left of x = 4, and P'(7, 3) is 3 squares right of it.

misconceptions.common: Answering 6, the distance between the point and its image. The mirror line is at the halfway point, not at the full distance.

questions.skill: reflecting in a vertical or horizontal line

questions.prompt: The grid shows the horizontal mirror line y = -2. Each point is reflected in this mirror line. Match each point to its image.
questions.solution: (0, 1) is 3 units above y = -2, so its image is 3 units below: (0, -5). (3, -4) is 2 units below y = -2, so its image is 2 units above: (3, 0). (-2, -2) is ON the mirror line, so it stays at (-2, -2).

misconceptions.common: Reflecting in the x-axis instead of the line y = -2, which gives (0, -1) and (3, 4). Always measure the distance from the given mirror line.

questions.skill: reflecting in a vertical or horizontal line

questions.prompt: Point P is plotted on the grid. It is reflected in the diagonal mirror line y = x shown. What are the coordinates of its image?
questions.solution: The diagonal mirror line y = x goes through (0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 2) and so on. In this mirror the x and y coordinates swap places. P(2, 5) becomes (5, 2). Check: both points are the same distance from the line, on opposite sides.

misconceptions.0: This is a reflection in the y-axis. The mirror here is the diagonal line y = x drawn on the grid.
misconceptions.2: This is a reflection in the x-axis. In this diagonal mirror, the point does not flip over an axis.
misconceptions.3: This uses the OTHER diagonal, the one through (1, -1) and (2, -2). For the line y = x drawn here, just swap the numbers.

questions.prompt: True or false: The point (4, 4) does not move when it is reflected in the diagonal mirror line y = x shown on the grid.
questions.solution: The mirror line y = x passes through every point whose two coordinates are equal: (0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (4, 4) and so on. (4, 4) is ON the mirror line, so it stays still. True.

misconceptions.common: Thinking every point must move. A point on the mirror line is its own image.

questions.prompt: Point P is plotted on the grid. It is reflected in the diagonal mirror line y = x shown. What are the coordinates of the image? Write them like (x, y).
questions.solution: In the mirror line y = x the two coordinates swap. P(6, 1) becomes (1, 6).

misconceptions.common: Changing a sign as if reflecting in an axis, for example writing (-6, 1). With this diagonal mirror the numbers swap places and keep their signs.

questions.prompt: Point P is plotted on the grid. Reflect P in the diagonal mirror line y = x drawn on the grid. Where is its image?
questions.solution: Swap the coordinates and keep their signs: P(-3, 1) becomes (1, -3). The point moves from the second quadrant to the fourth quadrant, on the other side of the diagonal mirror.

misconceptions.0: This swaps the numbers AND changes both signs, which is a reflection in the other diagonal (through (1, -1) and (2, -2)). For the mirror line y = x drawn here, just swap: (-3, 1) becomes (1, -3).
misconceptions.1: This is a reflection in the y-axis. A diagonal mirror swaps the coordinates.
misconceptions.2: This is a reflection in the x-axis. A diagonal mirror swaps the coordinates.

questions.prompt: Select ALL the points that lie on the diagonal mirror line that passes through (0, 0), (1, 1) and (2, 2). (The line carries on in both directions.)
questions.solution: Every point on this diagonal line has its x-coordinate equal to its y-coordinate. That includes negative and decimal values: (5, 5), (-2, -2) and (1.5, 1.5).

misconceptions.2: (2, -2) has different coordinates (2 and -2). It lies on the other diagonal, through (1, -1).
misconceptions.3: (0, 3) is on the y-axis, not on the diagonal. Its coordinates are not equal.
misconceptions.5: (3, 0) is on the x-axis, not on the diagonal. Its coordinates are not equal.

questions.prompt: Triangle ABC is drawn on the grid. It is reflected in the diagonal mirror line y = x shown. Where is the image of B?
questions.solution: B is at (3, 0). In the mirror line y = x the coordinates swap. B(3, 0) becomes (0, 3). B was on the x-axis, and its image is on the y-axis.

misconceptions.1: B is not on the mirror line (its coordinates 3 and 0 are not equal), so it must move.
misconceptions.2: This reflects B in the y-axis. In the diagonal mirror the coordinates swap.
misconceptions.3: This swaps the numbers but also changes a sign. That is the other diagonal mirror. For y = x, just swap: (3, 0) becomes (0, 3).

questions.prompt: Point P is plotted on the grid. True or false: when P is reflected in the diagonal mirror line y = x shown, its image is (-5, 2).
questions.solution: Swap the coordinates and keep their signs: P(-2, 5) becomes (5, -2), not (-5, 2). False.

misconceptions.common: Swapping the numbers but keeping the minus sign in the first place. The -2 moves to the second place, so the image is (5, -2).

questions.prompt: Point P is plotted on the grid. It is reflected in the diagonal mirror line y = -x shown, which slopes downwards from left to right. What are the coordinates of its image?
questions.solution: This mirror line goes through (0, 0), (1, -1), (2, -2) and so on. For this diagonal, swap the coordinates AND change both signs: P(3, 1) becomes (-1, -3). Check: halfway between (3, 1) and (-1, -3) is (1, -1), which is on the mirror line.

misconceptions.0: This uses the diagonal y = x (through (1, 1) and (2, 2)). The mirror drawn here goes through (1, -1) and (2, -2), so as well as swapping, both signs change.
misconceptions.1: Both signs have changed, but the numbers also need to swap places.
misconceptions.3: This is a reflection in the x-axis, not in a diagonal line.

questions.prompt: Point P is reflected in the diagonal mirror line y = x shown on the grid. Its image, P', is plotted. What were the coordinates of P? Write them like (x, y).
questions.solution: Reflecting in y = x swaps the coordinates, and reflecting back swaps them again. So P is (7, -4). Check: swapping (7, -4) gives (-4, 7), which is P'.

misconceptions.common: Changing the signs as well as swapping, which gives (-7, 4). With this diagonal mirror the signs stay with their numbers.

questions.prompt: Each point is reflected in the diagonal mirror line y = x drawn on the grid. Match each point to its image.
questions.solution: Swap the coordinates each time. (1, 3) becomes (3, 1). (-2, 0) becomes (0, -2). (5, -1) becomes (-1, 5).

misconceptions.common: Changing the signs as well as swapping (giving (-3, -1)), or reflecting in the y-axis (giving (2, 0)).

questions.prompt: The square drawn on the grid is reflected in the diagonal mirror line y = x shown. Which list gives the corners of the image?
questions.solution: Read the corners from the grid: (1, 2), (3, 2), (3, 4) and (1, 4). Swap the coordinates of every corner: (1, 2) to (2, 1), (3, 2) to (2, 3), (3, 4) to (4, 3), (1, 4) to (4, 1). The image is still a square with sides of 2 units, now on the other side of the diagonal.

misconceptions.0: This is a reflection in the y-axis. The diagonal mirror swaps the coordinates of each corner.
misconceptions.2: This is a reflection in the x-axis. The diagonal mirror swaps the coordinates of each corner.
misconceptions.3: This swaps the numbers and changes the signs, which is the other diagonal mirror (through (1, -1)). For y = x you only swap.

questions.prompt: Line OA is drawn on the grid. It is rotated 90° clockwise about O. Where does A go?
questions.solution: OA goes from O(0, 0) straight up to A(0, 3). Think of a clock hand pointing at 12. A quarter turn clockwise makes it point at 3, which is to the right. OA is still 3 units long, so A goes to (3, 0).

misconceptions.0: This is a 90° ANTICLOCKWISE turn. Clockwise is the way clock hands move: from 12 o'clock to 3 o'clock, which is from straight up to the right.
misconceptions.1: This is a half turn (180°). A 90° turn is only a quarter turn.
misconceptions.2: This slides A 3 units right instead of turning the line. When the line turns about O, it stays 3 units long and O stays at (0, 0).

questions.prompt: True or false: When a shape is rotated about one of its vertices (corners), that vertex stays in the same place.
questions.solution: The vertex you rotate about is the centre of rotation. The whole shape turns around it, like a door turning on its hinge, so that point does not move. True.

misconceptions.common: Thinking every point moves in a rotation. The centre of rotation is the one point that stays still.

questions.prompt: Line OB is drawn on the grid. It is rotated 90° anticlockwise about O. What are the coordinates of the image of B? Write them like (x, y).
questions.solution: OB goes from O(0, 0) to B(4, 0), pointing to the right. A quarter turn anticlockwise (the opposite way to clock hands) makes it point straight up. It is still 4 units long, so the image of B is (0, 4).

misconceptions.common: Turning clockwise instead, which gives (0, -4). Anticlockwise from pointing right means turning to point up.

questions.prompt: Triangle ABC is drawn on the grid. It is rotated 90° clockwise about A. What are the coordinates of the image of B?
questions.solution: A is at (1, 1) and B is at (4, 1), so AB goes 3 units right from A. A quarter turn clockwise turns 'right' into 'down'. So the image of B is 3 units DOWN from A: (1, 1 - 3) = (1, -2). A stays at (1, 1).

misconceptions.0: This is a 90° ANTICLOCKWISE rotation. Clockwise turns side AB (pointing right) to point DOWN.
misconceptions.1: This rotates about the origin (0, 0), not about A(1, 1). Use A as the centre.
misconceptions.3: This is a half turn (180°), so AB now points left. A 90° turn is only a quarter turn.

questions.prompt: Triangle ABC is drawn on the grid. It is rotated 90° anticlockwise about A. What are the coordinates of the image of C?
questions.solution: A is at (1, 1) and C is at (1, 3), so AC goes 2 units UP from A. A quarter turn anticlockwise turns 'up' into 'left'. So the image of C is 2 units LEFT of A: (1 - 2, 1) = (-1, 1).

misconceptions.1: This is a 90° CLOCKWISE rotation. Anticlockwise turns 'up' into 'left'.
misconceptions.2: This rotates about the origin (0, 0). The centre of rotation is A(1, 1).
misconceptions.3: This is a half turn (180°), so AC now points down. A 90° turn is a quarter turn.

questions.prompt: Rectangle PQRS is drawn on the grid. It is rotated 90° clockwise about P. What are the coordinates of the image of R? Write them like (x, y).
questions.solution: P is at (2, 1) and R is at (6, 3). From P to R you go 4 right and 2 up. Turn that movement a quarter turn clockwise: '4 right' becomes '4 down' and '2 up' becomes '2 right'. So from P go 2 right and 4 down: (2 + 2, 1 - 4) = (4, -3).

misconceptions.common: Turning anticlockwise instead (which gives (0, 5)), or only turning one part of the movement. Both the 'across' and the 'up' parts must turn.

questions.prompt: Triangle ABC and its image A'B'C' (dashed) are drawn on the grid. Which transformation maps ABC onto A'B'C'?
options: A reflection in the diagonal mirror line that passes through (0, 0), (1, 1) and (2, 2)
questions.solution: A and A' are the same point, (1, 1), so A is the centre. AB pointed right and A'B' points up: that is a quarter turn anticlockwise. Check C: from A, C(3, 2) is 2 right and 1 up. Turned anticlockwise this becomes 2 up and 1 left: (1 - 1, 1 + 2) = (0, 3). It matches C'.

misconceptions.0: A clockwise turn would send B (to the right of A) to a point BELOW A, at (1, -1). B' is above A.
misconceptions.1: This mirror does send A to (1, 1) and B to (1, 3), but it sends C(3, 2) to (2, 3), not (0, 3). Always check every corner.
misconceptions.2: A half turn would send B to (-1, 1), to the left of A. B' is above A, which is only a quarter turn.

questions.prompt: True or false: Rotating a shape 90° clockwise about a vertex gives the same image as rotating it 90° anticlockwise about the same vertex.
questions.solution: Clockwise and anticlockwise turn in opposite directions, so the images end up on opposite sides. For example, a line from (0, 0) to (2, 0) goes to (0, -2) when turned clockwise, but to (0, 2) when turned anticlockwise. False.

misconceptions.common: Thinking that only the size of the turn matters. The direction (clockwise or anticlockwise) is part of describing a rotation.

questions.prompt: The square on the grid is rotated 90° clockwise about its corner C. What are the coordinates of the image of corner D?
questions.solution: C is at (2, 0) and D is at (0, 2). From C, D is 2 left and 2 up. A quarter turn clockwise turns 'left' into 'up' and 'up' into 'right'. So the image is 2 up and 2 right of C: (2 + 2, 0 + 2) = (4, 2). The whole square swings over to the right, between x = 2 and x = 4.

misconceptions.0: This is an ANTICLOCKWISE turn. The square would swing down below the x-axis that way.
misconceptions.2: This is where the square's own corner C is. Rotating about the origin (0, 0) instead of about C would send D there. Use C(2, 0) as the centre.
misconceptions.3: This is a half turn (180°) about (2, 0). A 90° turn is only a quarter turn.

questions.prompt: Triangle PQR is drawn on the grid. It is rotated 90° anticlockwise about Q. What are the coordinates of the image of R?
questions.solution: Q is at (2, 2) and R is at (-1, 4). From Q, R is 3 left and 2 up. A quarter turn anticlockwise turns 'left' into 'down' and 'up' into 'left'. So the image is 3 down and 2 left of Q: (2 - 2, 2 - 3) = (0, -1).

misconceptions.0: This is a CLOCKWISE turn about Q. Anticlockwise turns 'left' into 'down'.
misconceptions.1: This rotates about the origin. The centre of rotation is Q(2, 2).
misconceptions.3: This is a half turn (180°) about Q. A 90° turn is a quarter turn.

questions.prompt: You are rotating a shape 90° clockwise about one of its corners using tracing paper. Put the steps in order, first to last.
options: Turn the tracing paper a quarter turn clockwise
Trace the shape onto the tracing paper
Join the marked corners to draw the image
Hold the chosen corner down with your pencil point
Mark where the corners of the traced shape are now
questions.solution: First trace the shape. Then pin the centre corner with your pencil so it cannot move. Turn the paper a quarter turn (90°) clockwise. Mark the new positions of the corners, then join them up to draw the image.

misconceptions.common: Turning the paper before holding the corner down. If the centre is not pinned first, the shape slides as well as turning.

questions.prompt: Line AB is drawn on the grid. It is rotated 90° clockwise about A. What is the x-coordinate of the image of B?
questions.solution: AB is 4 units long and points straight up from A(2, 1) to B(2, 5). A quarter turn clockwise makes it point right. So its end is 4 units right of A: (2 + 4, 1) = (6, 1). The x-coordinate is 6.

misconceptions.common: Answering -2 by turning anticlockwise (the line would then point left, to (-2, 1)), or answering 4 by giving the length of the line instead of the coordinate.

questions.prompt: Triangle ABC is rotated 90° clockwise about its vertex A. A and B', the image of vertex B, are plotted on the grid. What were the coordinates of B before the rotation? Write them like (x, y).
questions.solution: A is at (2, 2) and B' is at (5, 2), so B' is 3 units right of A. To undo a clockwise quarter turn, turn back anticlockwise: 'right' turns into 'up'. So B was 3 units UP from A: (2, 2 + 3) = (2, 5). Check: turning (2, 5) clockwise about (2, 2) points the line right, to (5, 2).

misconceptions.common: Turning (5, 2) clockwise again, which gives (2, -1). To find the original, you must turn the opposite way.

questions.prompt: Match each transformation to its description.

right: a slide with no turning or flipping
a flip over a mirror line
a turn about a fixed point

questions.solution: A reflection flips a shape over a mirror line. A rotation turns a shape about a fixed point (the centre of rotation). A translation slides a shape without turning or flipping it. None of them changes the size.

misconceptions.common: Mixing up rotation and reflection. Remember: rotate = turn (like a wheel), reflect = flip (like a mirror), translate = slide.

questions.prompt: The picture shows a toy windmill from the front. Its 4 blades are identical and equally spaced around the centre. What is the order of rotational symmetry of the windmill?

diagram.alt: A toy windmill seen from the front: 4 identical triangular blades arranged around a small square centre.

questions.solution: Imagine turning the windmill in the picture about its centre. Each blade moves into the next blade's place after a quarter turn (90°), so it looks the same 4 times in one full turn. Order of rotational symmetry = 4.

misconceptions.0: Order 1 means the shape only looks the same after a full turn. The windmill looks the same after every quarter turn, so its order is higher.
misconceptions.1: The windmill looks the same after a half turn, but also after each quarter turn. Count every position in one full turn where it looks the same.
misconceptions.3: This counts the blades and the gaps between them. Only count the positions in one full turn where the whole windmill looks exactly the same: 4.

questions.prompt: True or false: A pattern that only looks the same after a full turn of 360° has rotational symmetry of order 0.
questions.solution: Every shape looks the same after a full turn, so the smallest possible order is 1. A pattern that only fits onto itself after a full turn has rotational symmetry of order 1, not 0. False.

misconceptions.common: Thinking 'no rotational symmetry' means order 0. We describe it as order 1, because the full turn always counts once.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the transformation that flips a shape over a mirror line?
questions.solution: Flipping a shape over a mirror line is called a reflection. The image is a mirror image of the original.

misconceptions.common: Writing 'rotation'. A rotation turns a shape; a reflection flips it.

questions.prompt: Siti draws half of a shape on the grid. She completes the shape so that the y-axis (the dashed line) is a line of symmetry. Which of these points must also be a corner of the completed shape?
questions.solution: The y-axis is the mirror line, so every corner has a partner on the other side at the same height. The top right corner of Siti's half is (3, 5). It is 3 squares right of the y-axis, so its partner is 3 squares left: (-3, 5). (The other new corners are (-1, 2) and (-3, 2).)

misconceptions.0: This reflects (3, 5) in the x-axis. The line of symmetry here is the y-axis, so the shape is completed on the LEFT side.
misconceptions.2: This swaps the coordinates, which is a reflection in a diagonal line, not the y-axis.
misconceptions.3: Only the x-coordinate changes sign when reflecting in the y-axis. The height (y = 5) stays the same.

questions.prompt: Select ALL the transformations that always give an image exactly the same size and shape as the original.
options: Enlarging the shape to twice its size
Stretching the shape to make it twice as wide
questions.solution: Reflections (flips), rotations (turns) and translations (slides) only move a shape. Its size, angles and side lengths stay exactly the same. Enlarging and stretching change the size.

misconceptions.3: An enlargement keeps the shape but makes it bigger, so the size changes.
misconceptions.4: Stretching in one direction changes both the size and the shape (a square would become a rectangle).

questions.prompt: Triangle ABC and its image A'B'C' (dashed) are drawn on the grid. Which single transformation maps ABC onto A'B'C'?
questions.solution: Read the corners from the grid and compare each one with its image: A(1, 1) to A'(-1, 1), B(3, 1) to B'(-3, 1), C(1, 2) to C'(-1, 2). The y-coordinates are unchanged and every x-coordinate has changed sign. The triangle has flipped over the y-axis, so it is a reflection in the y-axis. Check all three corners, not just one.

misconceptions.0: This does move A(1, 1) to (-1, 1), but it moves B(3, 1) to (1, 1), not to (-3, 1). Check every corner.
misconceptions.1: That would change the signs of the y-coordinates, sending A to (1, -1). Here the y-coordinates stay the same and the x-coordinates change sign.
misconceptions.2: This does send A(1, 1) to (-1, 1), but it sends B(3, 1) to (-1, 3), not (-3, 1). Check every corner.

questions.prompt: The badge design shown has 3 identical petals equally spaced around its centre. What is the order of rotational symmetry of the design?

diagram.alt: A badge design made of 3 identical pointed petals arranged around its centre.

questions.solution: Imagine turning the badge about its centre. Each petal moves into the next petal's place after one third of a full turn (120°). That happens 3 times in a full turn, so the order of rotational symmetry is 3.

misconceptions.1: The design fits onto itself after one third of a turn, not only after a full turn, so its order is more than 1.
misconceptions.2: This counts the petals and the gaps. Only count the positions in one full turn where the whole design looks the same: 3.
misconceptions.3: A half turn would move a petal to where a gap is, so the design does not look the same after a half turn.

questions.prompt: True or false: A pattern can have rotational symmetry of order 4 but no lines of symmetry at all.
questions.solution: Think of a pinwheel with 4 identical arms, each bent the same way round. It looks the same after every quarter turn, so it has order 4. But if you fold it along any line, the bent arms point the wrong way and do not match, so it has no lines of symmetry. True.

misconceptions.common: Thinking that rotational symmetry and line symmetry always come together. A square has both, but a pinwheel shape has only rotational symmetry.

questions.prompt: The tile pattern shown is a square with an identical small triangle on the middle of its top side and of its bottom side. The other two sides are plain. What is the order of rotational symmetry of the whole pattern?

diagram.alt: A tile pattern: a square with one small triangle on the middle of its top side and an identical triangle on the middle of its bottom side. The left and right sides are plain.

questions.solution: Try each turn. A quarter turn (90°) moves the triangles to the sides, so it does not match. A half turn (180°) swaps the top and bottom triangles, so it matches. A full turn matches. It fits onto itself twice in one full turn: order 2.

misconceptions.1: A plain square has order 4, but after a quarter turn the triangles would be on the left and right instead of the top and bottom, so the pattern does not look the same.
misconceptions.2: After a half turn, the top triangle moves to the bottom and the bottom one moves to the top. The pattern looks the same, so the order is more than 1.
misconceptions.3: This counts the pieces (one square and two triangles). The order counts how many times the pattern looks the same in one full turn.

questions.prompt: A dot pattern on a coordinate grid has BOTH the x-axis and the y-axis as lines of symmetry. One of its dots is at (3, 2). Select ALL the points that must also be dots in the pattern.
questions.solution: Reflect (3, 2) in the y-axis: (-3, 2). Reflect (3, 2) in the x-axis: (3, -2). The dot (-3, 2) must also be reflected in the x-axis: (-3, -2). So there is a dot in every quadrant: (3, 2), (-3, 2), (3, -2) and (-3, -2).

misconceptions.3: (2, 3) swaps the coordinates, which is a reflection in the diagonal line. The diagonal is not one of the lines of symmetry here.
misconceptions.4: (-2, -3) swaps the coordinates as well as changing the signs. The lines of symmetry are the axes, so the numbers stay in their places.

questions.prompt: Triangle ABC is drawn on the grid. It is reflected in the mirror line x = 1. What are the coordinates of C', the image of C? Write them like (x, y).
questions.solution: C is at (5, 4). The mirror line x = 1 is vertical, so only the x-coordinate changes. C is 5 - 1 = 4 squares to the right of the mirror, so C' is 4 squares to the left of it: x = 1 - 4 = -3. The height stays the same (y = 4). C' = (-3, 4).

misconceptions.common: It looks like you reflected C in the y-axis and got (-5, 4). The mirror here is the dashed line x = 1, so count the squares from that line, not from the y-axis.

questions.skill: reflecting in a vertical or horizontal line

questions.prompt: Trapezium PQRS is drawn on the grid. It is reflected in the mirror line y = 3. Where is R', the image of R?
questions.solution: R is at (4, 6). The mirror line y = 3 is horizontal, so only the y-coordinate changes. R is 6 - 3 = 3 squares above the mirror, so R' is 3 squares below it: y = 3 - 3 = 0. x stays 4. R' = (4, 0). R is on the edge furthest from the mirror, so R' is also furthest from the mirror on the other side.

misconceptions.0: It looks like you slid the trapezium down below the mirror without flipping it. In a reflection the shape flips over: R is on the top edge, furthest from the mirror, so R' must be furthest from the mirror on the other side, 3 squares below y = 3.
misconceptions.1: This reflects R in the x-axis. The mirror here is the dashed line y = 3, so measure 3 squares from that line, not 6 from the x-axis.
misconceptions.3: This reflects R in the y-axis, which is a vertical mirror. The line y = 3 is horizontal, so R moves straight down and keeps x = 4.

questions.skill: reflecting in a vertical or horizontal line

questions.prompt: Triangle JKL is drawn on the grid. It is reflected in the diagonal mirror line y = x shown. What are the coordinates of J', the image of J? Write them like (x, y).
questions.solution: J is at (-3, 1). In the mirror line y = x the two coordinates swap places and keep their signs. So (-3, 1) becomes (1, -3). Check: J is above the mirror line and J' is below it, and the point halfway between them, (-1, -1), is on the mirror line.

misconceptions.common: It looks like you changed a sign as well as swapping, for example writing (-1, 3). In the mirror line y = x, just swap the numbers and keep each sign with its number: (-3, 1) becomes (1, -3).

questions.prompt: Triangle ABC is reflected in a vertical mirror line. Its image is the dashed triangle A'B'C' on the grid. Which line is the mirror line?
questions.solution: The mirror line is exactly halfway between each point and its image. A is at x = 3 and A' is at x = 1, so halfway is x = 2. Check B: B is at x = 6 and B' is at x = -2, and halfway is (6 + (-2)) / 2 = 2. The mirror line is x = 2.

misconceptions.0: x = 1 is the line through A' and C', an edge of the image. The mirror line is halfway between A and A', at x = 2, so the triangle and its image are both 1 square away from it.
misconceptions.2: x = 3 is the line through A and C, an edge of the triangle. The mirror line lies halfway between the triangle and its image, at x = 2.
misconceptions.3: y = 2 is a horizontal line (the bottom edges lie on it). The triangle has flipped from right to left, so the mirror line is vertical: it is an x = line.

questions.skill: reflecting in a vertical or horizontal line

questions.prompt: Shape S is reflected in a mirror line. Its image is the dashed shape on the grid. Which line is the mirror line?
questions.solution: Match the corners. (1, 3) goes to (-3, -1), (1, 5) goes to (-5, -1) and (2, 5) goes to (-5, -2). Each time the numbers swap places AND both signs change. That is a reflection in the diagonal line through (0, 0), (1, -1) and (2, -2). Check one pair: halfway between (1, 3) and (-3, -1) is (-1, 1), which is on that line.

misconceptions.0: A reflection in the x-axis would keep the shape on the right (x stays 1 and 2) and move it below the axis. The image here is on the left AND below, and its corners have swapped numbers.
misconceptions.1: A reflection in the y-axis would keep the shape at the same height (y from 3 to 5). The image is below the x-axis, so the mirror is not the y-axis.
misconceptions.2: The diagonal through (1, 1) swaps the numbers but keeps the signs, so (1, 3) would go to (3, 1), still in the first quadrant. Here (1, 3) goes to (-3, -1): the signs change too, so it is the other diagonal.

questions.prompt: Trapezium PQRS is drawn on the grid. It is rotated 90° clockwise about vertex Q. What are the coordinates of the image of S? Write them like (x, y).
questions.solution: Q is at (4, 1) and S is at (1, 3). From Q, S is 3 squares left and 2 squares up. A quarter turn clockwise turns 'left' into 'up' and 'up' into 'right'. So the image of S is 3 up and 2 right of Q: (4 + 2, 1 + 3) = (6, 4).

misconceptions.common: It looks like you turned anticlockwise, which gives (2, -2). Clockwise is the way clock hands move: side QP, which points left, turns to point up.

questions.prompt: Triangle DEF is drawn on the grid. It is rotated 90° anticlockwise about vertex E. Match each vertex to the coordinates of its image.
questions.solution: E is the centre, so it stays at (1, 1). From E, D(-2, 1) is 3 squares left; a quarter turn anticlockwise turns 'left' into 'down', so D goes 3 squares below E: (1, -2). From E, F(1, 3) is 2 squares up; anticlockwise turns 'up' into 'left', so F goes 2 squares left of E: (-1, 1).

misconceptions.common: Turning clockwise instead, which sends D to (1, 4) and F to (3, 1). Anticlockwise is the opposite way to clock hands: a side pointing up turns to point left.

questions.prompt: Shape A is drawn on the grid. The dashed shape is its image. Which transformation maps shape A onto its image?
questions.solution: Compare the two shapes. The image is the same size and faces the same way: the long side is still along the bottom and the right angle is still at the bottom left. Every corner has moved 4 squares right and 2 squares up. Sliding without turning or flipping is a translation.

misconceptions.1: A reflection flips the shape, so the right angle would end up on the other side, like a mirror picture. Here the image faces exactly the same way as shape A.
misconceptions.2: A rotation turns the shape, so its sides would point in new directions. Here the long side is still along the bottom.
misconceptions.3: An enlargement changes the size. The image is exactly the same size as shape A.

questions.prompt: Triangle ABC is drawn on the grid. The dashed triangle is its image after one transformation. Which transformation was it?
options: A rotation of 90° anticlockwise about A
A rotation of 90° clockwise about A
questions.solution: Corner A has not moved, so the triangle has turned about A. Side AB pointed right, from A(2, 1) to B(5, 1). In the image the matching side points straight up from A, to (2, 4). Turning from 'right' to 'up' is a quarter turn anticlockwise. Check C: from A, C is 3 right and 1 up; turned anticlockwise this becomes 3 up and 1 left: (2 - 1, 1 + 3) = (1, 4), which is a corner of the image. So it is a rotation of 90° anticlockwise about A.

misconceptions.0: A translation slides the shape without turning it, so side AB would still point right. In the image it points up, and corner A has not moved at all.
misconceptions.1: A reflection makes a mirror picture, back to front. Imagine tracing triangle ABC and turning the tracing a quarter turn anticlockwise about A: it lands exactly on the dashed triangle without flipping the paper over, so this is a rotation.
misconceptions.3: A clockwise quarter turn would make side AB point DOWN from A, to (2, -2). In the image it points up, which is anticlockwise.

questions.prompt: Which grid shows the correct reflection of shape P in the mirror line? The dashed shape is the image.
questions.solution: In a reflection every corner ends up the same distance from the mirror line, on the other side, and the shape is flipped like a mirror picture. Shape P's tall side is 3 squares left of the mirror line, so in the image the tall side is 3 squares right of it. Shape P's short side is 1 square from the mirror, so the image's short side is also 1 square from it. Only Grid A shows this.

misconceptions.1: In Grid B the shape has slid across without flipping: its tall side is still on the left. A reflection is a mirror picture, so the tall side must be on the right, furthest from the mirror.
misconceptions.2: In Grid C the shape is flipped, but it touches the mirror line. Shape P is 1 square away from the mirror, so its image must also be 1 square away on the other side.
misconceptions.3: In Grid D the shape has been turned upside down. A vertical mirror flips a shape from left to right only: the flat bottom edge stays at the bottom.

questions.skill: reflecting in a vertical or horizontal line

questions.prompt: Which grid shows shape P rotated 90° clockwise about the marked corner? The dashed shape is the image.
questions.solution: Use the marked corner (3, 3) as the centre. The bottom edge of P goes 3 squares right from the centre. A quarter turn clockwise turns 'right' into 'down', so in the image this edge goes 3 squares down from the centre, to (3, 0). Only Grid B has the image hanging below the centre like that, and its other corners match too: (6, 4) goes to (4, 0) and (4, 5) goes to (5, 2).

misconceptions.0: Grid A shows a quarter turn ANTICLOCKWISE: the bottom edge now points up. Clockwise is the way clock hands move, so an edge pointing right turns to point down.
misconceptions.2: Grid C shows a half turn (180°): the bottom edge now points left. A 90° turn is only a quarter turn, so the edge should point down.
misconceptions.3: Grid D shows a reflection in an upright line through the marked corner: the shape is flipped, not turned. Tracing paper turned a quarter turn clockwise never flips the shape over.

questions.prompt: Which grid shows the reflection of triangle T in the diagonal mirror line y = x? The dashed triangle is the image.
questions.solution: In the mirror line y = x every corner's coordinates swap places. T has corners (1, 3), (1, 6) and (3, 6), so the image has corners (3, 1), (6, 1) and (6, 3). Grid D shows this triangle. Check: (1, 3) and (3, 1) are the same distance from the mirror line, on opposite sides.

misconceptions.0: In Grid A the triangle has slid down and to the right without flipping: its long side still stands upright. In the diagonal mirror the upright long side of T becomes a flat side along the bottom of the image.
misconceptions.1: Grid B shows a reflection in an upright (vertical) mirror line, not in the diagonal. In the diagonal mirror the coordinates swap, so (1, 3) goes to (3, 1).
misconceptions.2: Grid C has the right shape the right way round, but it is one square too far to the right: (1, 3) would go to (4, 1). The image must be the same distance from the mirror line as T, so just swap the coordinates.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows an equilateral triangle. What is its order of rotational symmetry?
questions.solution: An equilateral triangle has 3 equal sides and 3 equal angles. Turn it about its centre: it fits onto its own outline after every third of a turn (120°, 240° and 360°). That is 3 times in one full turn, so the order of rotational symmetry is 3.

misconceptions.common: Answering 1 or 2. A half turn does not work for a triangle (a corner would point down), but a third of a turn does. Count every position in one full turn where the triangle fits exactly onto its outline: there are 3.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows a parallelogram that is not a rectangle. What is its order of rotational symmetry?
questions.solution: Turn the parallelogram about its centre. After a quarter turn (90°) its long sides would stand upright, so it does not fit its outline. After a half turn (180°) it fits exactly: the two long sides swap places, and so do the two slanting sides. Together with the full turn, that is 2 positions. Order = 2.

misconceptions.0: A square has order 4, but a parallelogram does not fit onto itself after a quarter turn: its long sides would end up standing upright.
misconceptions.1: Order 1 means it only fits after a full turn. Try a half turn: the parallelogram lands exactly on its own outline, so the order is more than 1.
misconceptions.3: Order 3 belongs to shapes like an equilateral triangle. A parallelogram fits onto itself only after a half turn and a full turn: order 2.

questions.prompt: True or false: The rectangle shown (it is not a square) has rotational symmetry of order 4.
questions.solution: After a quarter turn (90°) the rectangle would stand on its short side, so it does not fit its outline. A half turn (180°) and a full turn do fit. That is order 2, not 4. False.

misconceptions.common: Thinking a rectangle behaves like a square because all its angles are right angles. A square fits after every quarter turn; a rectangle only after a half turn, because its sides are not all equal.

questions.prompt: What is the order of rotational symmetry of a square?
questions.solution: Turn a square around its centre. It looks the same after 90°, 180°, 270° and 360°. That is 4 times, so the order is 4.

misconceptions.1: You counted only the half turn. A square also fits after a quarter turn and a three-quarter turn, as well as the full turn: 4 times.
misconceptions.2: You added the 4 lines of symmetry to the 4 turns. The order only counts how many times the shape fits onto itself in one full turn.
misconceptions.3: 90° is the angle of each turn, not the order. The order is the number of times it fits in a full turn: 360 ÷ 90 = 4.

questions.prompt: True or false: A shape with rotational symmetry of order 1 only looks the same after a full turn of 360°.
questions.solution: Every shape looks the same after a full turn. If that is the ONLY time it fits onto itself, its order is 1, which means it has no rotational symmetry. The statement is true.

misconceptions.common: Thinking order 1 means the shape has some special symmetry. Order 1 really means no rotational symmetry.

questions.prompt: Shapes A, B, C and D are drawn on the squared grid. Shape B is an equilateral triangle. Match each shape to its order of rotational symmetry.
questions.solution: A is a kite (two pairs of equal sides next to each other): it fits onto itself only after a full turn, so order 1. B, equilateral triangle: fits after 120°, 240° and 360°, so order 3. C is a square (4 by 4): fits after every quarter turn, order 4. D is a rectangle (6 by 3, not a square): fits after 180° and 360°, order 2.

misconceptions.common: Giving the kite (shape A) order 2 because it has a line of symmetry. A kite only fits onto itself after a full turn, so its order is 1. And the rectangle (shape D) is not a square, so it does not fit after a quarter turn: order 2, not 4.

questions.prompt: A capital letter H is drawn with two equal upright lines joined by a crossbar exactly in the middle. What is its order of rotational symmetry?
questions.solution: Turn the H halfway round (180°). It looks exactly the same. After a full turn it fits again. So it fits 2 times in a full turn: order 2.

misconceptions.common: Answering 1 because the H does not fit after a quarter turn. It does fit after a half turn, so its order is 2.

questions.skill: rotational symmetry of letters and patterns

questions.prompt: Select ALL the capital letters (written in plain block capitals) that have rotational symmetry of order 2.
questions.solution: Turn each letter halfway round (180°). H, N and Z look exactly the same, so they have order 2. A, T and E do not, so they have order 1 (even though A, T and E have lines of symmetry).

misconceptions.2: A has a line of symmetry, but upside down it does not look like A, so its order is 1.
misconceptions.4: T upside down is not T, so its order is 1.
misconceptions.5: E has a line of symmetry across the middle, but after a half turn it faces the other way, so its order is 1.

questions.skill: rotational symmetry of letters and patterns

questions.prompt: A pattern looks exactly the same after a quarter turn (90°), and it does not look the same after any smaller turn. What is its order of rotational symmetry?
questions.solution: If it fits after a quarter turn, it fits after every quarter turn: 90°, 180°, 270° and 360°. That is 4 times, so the order is 4.

misconceptions.0: You counted only the first quarter turn. It fits after 90°, 180°, 270° and 360°.
misconceptions.1: You counted only the half turn and the full turn. It also fits after 90° and 270°.
misconceptions.2: 90 is the angle of the turn, not the order. Order = 360 ÷ 90 = 4.

questions.prompt: The drawing shows a ceiling fan seen from below. It has 3 identical blades, evenly spaced, so its order of rotational symmetry is 3. What is the smallest angle you must turn it through so that it looks the same again? Give your answer in degrees.

diagram.alt: A ceiling fan seen from below: three identical blades spaced evenly round the centre.

questions.solution: A full turn is 360°. The fan fits onto itself 3 times in a full turn (once for each blade), so each turn is 360 ÷ 3 = 120°.

misconceptions.common: Using 90° (a quarter turn) for every shape. The angle depends on the order: 360 ÷ order = 360 ÷ 3 = 120°.

questions.skill: rotational symmetry of letters and patterns

questions.prompt: The shape drawn is an isosceles trapezium (its two sloping sides are equal). What is its order of rotational symmetry?
questions.solution: Turn the trapezium about its centre. After a half turn the long side would be at the top, so it does not fit. It only looks the same after a full turn, so its order of rotational symmetry is 1. (It has 1 line of symmetry, but that is a different kind of symmetry.)

misconceptions.common: If you said 0: every shape fits onto itself after a full turn, so the smallest order is 1. If you said 2: the trapezium has a line of symmetry, but a half turn puts the long side at the top, so it does not fit.

questions.prompt: Look at the four shapes. Shape C is an equilateral triangle and shape D is a square. Which shape has rotational symmetry of order 2?
questions.solution: Shape A is a parallelogram. Turn it halfway round (180°) about its centre and it fits onto itself; it fits again after a full turn. That is 2 times, so its order is 2. Shape B (a kite) has order 1, the equilateral triangle C has order 3 and the square D has order 4.

misconceptions.1: Shape B is a kite. It has one line of symmetry, but it only fits onto itself after a full turn, so its order is 1.
misconceptions.2: The equilateral triangle fits onto itself 3 times in a full turn (every 120°), so its order is 3, not 2.
misconceptions.3: The square fits onto itself after every quarter turn, 4 times in all, so its order is 4, not 2.

questions.prompt: The shape drawn is a rectangle that is not a square. What is the smallest angle you must turn it through, about its centre, so that it looks exactly the same again? Give your answer in degrees.
questions.solution: After a quarter turn (90°) the long sides would be upright, so the rectangle does not fit. After a half turn (180°) it fits exactly. So the smallest angle is 180°, and the order of rotational symmetry is 2 (360 ÷ 180 = 2).

misconceptions.common: If you said 90°, you used a quarter turn for every shape. A rectangle that is not a square only fits again after a half turn: 180°. If you said 2, that is the order, not the angle.

questions.skill: rotational symmetry of letters and patterns

questions.prompt: Shape P touches the mirror line x = -1. Which grid shows the reflection of shape P in the mirror line x = -1? The dashed shape is the image.
questions.solution: Step 1: P's upright side, from (-1, 1) to (-1, 4), lies ON the mirror line, so it does not move. Step 2: corner (2, 1) is 3 squares right of x = -1, so its image is 3 squares left of the line: (-4, 1). Step 3: corner (3, 3) is 4 squares right of the line, so its image is (-5, 3). Step 4: the image shares the upright side with P and is flipped over, like a mirror picture. Grid C shows this. Trap: the mirror is x = -1, not the y-axis.

misconceptions.0: This image is the reflection in the y-axis (the line x = 0), not in x = -1. Use the dashed line x = -1 as the mirror: count each corner's distance from THAT line, then count the same distance on the other side.
misconceptions.1: This shape has been slid to the left without flipping: its upright side is now on the far left. In a reflection the upright side of P lies on the mirror line, so it stays exactly where it is and the shape flips over it.
misconceptions.3: This image is flipped the right way, but it is 1 square too far from the mirror line, so there is a gap. P touches the mirror line, so its image must touch it too: each corner is the same distance from x = -1 on the other side.

questions.skill: reflecting in a vertical or horizontal line

questions.prompt: Quadrilateral ABCD crosses the diagonal mirror line y = x drawn on the grid. It is reflected in the mirror line. Match each corner to the coordinates of its image.
questions.solution: Read the corners: A(1, 1), B(4, 1), C(5, 3), D(2, 4). In the mirror line y = x the two coordinates of each point swap places. A is ON the mirror line, so it stays at (1, 1). B goes to (1, 4) and C goes to (3, 5). D is on the other side of the line, but the rule is the same: (2, 4) goes to (4, 2). So the image crosses the line too. Trap: do not change any signs; that is a different mirror line.

misconceptions.common: For the mirror line y = x, just swap the two numbers of each corner; do not make them negative (that would be the other diagonal). A corner on the mirror line, like A, does not move, and a corner on the other side, like D(2, 4), still swaps: (4, 2).

questions.prompt: Quadrilateral ABCD is reflected in a mirror line. Its image A'B'C'D' is the dashed shape on the grid; corner A does not move. Mei Lin says: "A is on the diagonal line y = x and it did not move, so the mirror line is y = x." Is she correct? Tick one.
options: Yes. A point on the mirror line does not move, and A is on the line y = x.
No. B(5, 3) goes to B'(5, 1); halfway between them is y = 2, so the mirror line is y = 2.
Yes. The image is exactly the same size and shape as ABCD.
No. The image is below ABCD, so the mirror line must be the x-axis.
questions.solution: Step 1: A not moving only tells you A is on the mirror line. Step 2: check another corner. B is (5, 3) and B' is (5, 1): same x, so the mirror line is horizontal. Step 3: halfway between y = 3 and y = 1 is y = 2. Step 4: check C: (4, 5) is 3 above y = 2 and C'(4, -1) is 3 below. The mirror line is y = 2, so Mei Lin is wrong. Trap: one corner that fits is not enough.

misconceptions.0: A did not move, but that only shows A is on the mirror line. Many lines pass through A. Check another corner: in y = x, B(5, 3) would go to (3, 5), but B' is at (5, 1). Always check more than one corner.
misconceptions.2: Every reflection keeps the size and shape, whatever the mirror line, so this reason cannot show WHICH line it is. Check where the corners go.
misconceptions.3: In the x-axis, B(5, 3) would go to (5, -3), but B' is at (5, 1). The mirror line is exactly halfway between a point and its image: halfway between y = 3 and y = 1 is y = 2.

questions.skill: reflecting in a vertical or horizontal line

questions.prompt: Quadrilateral ABCD is drawn on the grid. It is rotated 90° clockwise about vertex B. Match each of the corners A, C and D to the coordinates of its image.
questions.solution: B(1, 1) is the centre, so it stays put. Work from B to each corner, then turn that move a quarter turn clockwise (right becomes down, up becomes right, left becomes up). A is 4 left of B, so A' is 4 up: (1, 5). C is 2 up, so C' is 2 right: (3, 1). D is 3 left and 3 up, so D' is 3 up and 3 right: (4, 4). Check: each corner stays the same distance from B.

misconceptions.common: Turning anticlockwise instead, which sends A to (1, -3), C to (-1, 1) and D to (-2, -2); or making a half turn, which sends A to (5, 1). Clockwise is the way clock hands go: an arm from B that points left turns to point up.

questions.prompt: Shape PQRS has been rotated 90° about one of its own corners. Its image is the dashed shape on the grid. Which rotation was it?
questions.solution: Step 1: the image has corners at P(2, 1) and at S(2, 4), so the centre could be P or S. Step 2: test P as the centre. PQ is 3 squares right of P; the image has a side 3 squares UP from P, to (2, 4). Right turning to up is a quarter turn anticlockwise. Step 3: check R: from P it is 3 right and 2 up; turned anticlockwise that is 3 up and 2 left: (0, 4), a corner of the image. Step 4: S was 3 up; it turns to 3 left: (-1, 1). It all fits: 90° anticlockwise about P. Trap: the corner at S's place is Q', not S.

misconceptions.0: The centre is right, but check the direction. From P, side PQ pointed right; in the image the matching side points up. Right to up is a quarter turn ANTICLOCKWISE (against the clock hands).
misconceptions.1: The image has a corner where S is, but that corner is the image of Q, not S. If the turn were about S, S would stay put and P would swing to (5, 4), and the image has no corner there. Find the corner whose OWN image is itself: P.
misconceptions.2: If the turn were clockwise about S, P would swing to (-1, 4), and the image has no corner there. The corner at S's place is really the image of Q. The centre is P, and the turn is anticlockwise.

questions.prompt: Triangle ABC is drawn on the grid. One dashed triangle is ABC rotated 90° about A. The other is ABC reflected in a line through A. Which statement names the rotation AND gives a reason that proves it is the rotation? Tick one.
options: X. Side AB pointed right and in X it points down; side AC pointed up and in X it points right. Each side from A has turned a quarter turn clockwise.
Y, because Y is exactly the same size and shape as ABC.
Y, because corner A has not moved.
X, because it is below triangle ABC and the same size.
questions.solution: Step 1: in a rotation about A, every side from A turns through the same quarter turn. Step 2: in X, AB (3 squares right) has become 3 squares down, and AC (2 squares up) has become 2 squares right. Both turned a quarter turn clockwise, so X is the rotation. Step 3: in Y, AB has flipped to point left but AC still points up: one side turned and one did not, so Y is a reflection (in x = 3). Trap: 'same size and shape', 'A has not moved' and 'it is below' are true or nearly true for both, so they are not reasons.

misconceptions.1: X and Y are both the same size and shape as ABC: rotations and reflections both keep size and shape. So this reason cannot tell them apart. Y is the reflection (in the line x = 3): it is flipped, not turned.
misconceptions.2: A has not moved in X either: a rotation about A and a reflection in a line through A both keep A still. Look at how each side has moved: in Y, side AB has flipped to point left, which a quarter turn cannot do.
misconceptions.3: X is the rotation, but 'below' does not prove it: a reflection in the line y = 2 through A would also land below ABC. A full answer says how the sides have turned: right became down and up became right.

questions.prompt: Look at the six shapes. Select ALL the shapes that have rotational symmetry of order 2.
questions.solution: Turn each shape about its centre and count how many times it fits onto itself in one full turn. A (rectangle, not a square): after a half turn and a full turn, so order 2. B (square): after every quarter turn, so order 4, not 2. C (the Z shape): after a half turn and a full turn, order 2, even though it has no line of symmetry. D (kite) and F (trapezium): only after a full turn, order 1. E (rhombus, not a square): order 2. Answer: A, C and E.

misconceptions.1: The square does fit after a half turn, but it also fits after every quarter turn: 4 times in a full turn. Its order is 4, not 2.
misconceptions.3: The kite has a line of symmetry, but after a half turn its long point is at the top. It only fits after a full turn, so its order is 1.
misconceptions.5: The trapezium has a line of symmetry, but after a half turn the short side is at the bottom. It only fits after a full turn, so its order is 1.
misconceptions.common: Order 2 means the shape fits onto itself exactly 2 times in a full turn: after the half turn and the full turn. Line symmetry is a different thing: the Z shape has no lines of symmetry but still has order 2.

questions.prompt: The shaded pattern on the grid is turned about the marked centre. What is the smallest angle it must turn through to look exactly the same again? Give your answer in degrees.

diagram.alt: A shaded pattern on a grid: a 2 by 2 square on the marked centre with four arms. The arm to the right and the arm to the left are each 3 squares long; the arm going up and the arm going down are each 2 squares long.

questions.solution: Step 1: try a quarter turn (90°). The right arm is 3 squares long, but it would turn into the place of the up arm, which is only 2 squares long. So 90° does not work. Step 2: try a half turn (180°). The right arm goes to the left arm (both 3 long) and the up arm goes to the down arm (both 2 long). It fits. The smallest angle is 180° (order 2).

misconceptions.common: Answering 90° because the pattern has four arms. Check the arm lengths: the left and right arms are 3 squares long, the up and down arms only 2. After a quarter turn they would not match, so you need a half turn: 180°.

questions.prompt: Kumar wants the pattern on the grid to have rotational symmetry of order 2 about the marked centre. He shades as few extra squares as possible. Select ALL the lettered squares he must shade.
questions.solution: Step 1: for order 2, every shaded square needs a partner after a half turn about the centre: the same distance away on the exact opposite side. Step 2: the two squares touching the centre corner to corner are already partners, so they need nothing. Step 3: a half turn sends the middle of a square from (a, b) to (6 - a, 6 - b), because the centre is (3, 3). The shaded square with its middle at (4.5, 3.5) goes to (1.5, 2.5): square A. The one at (5.5, 4.5) goes to (0.5, 1.5): square D. The one at (1.5, 3.5) goes to (4.5, 2.5): square E. Answer: A, D and E. Trap: B and C are mirror images, not half-turn images, and F is a quarter turn.

misconceptions.1: Square B is where the top-right square would go in a vertical mirror line through the centre. A half turn sends a square to the OPPOSITE side, both across and down.
misconceptions.2: Square C is where the top-right square would go in a horizontal mirror line through the centre. A half turn moves it across AND down, to the opposite side of the centre: square D.
misconceptions.5: Square F is where the top-right square would go after a quarter turn. Order 2 needs a half turn (180°), not a quarter turn.
misconceptions.common: Turn the page upside down in your head: each shaded square must land on another shaded square. Two squares that are already opposite each other through the centre need nothing extra.

questions.prompt: Siti starts with the L-shaped piece shaded in the top right of each grid. She adds more pieces so that her pattern has rotational symmetry of order 4 about the marked centre. Which grid shows her finished pattern?
questions.solution: Step 1: order 4 means the pattern fits onto itself after every quarter turn (90°, 180°, 270°, 360°). Step 2: so the pattern must contain the L, the L turned a quarter turn, a half turn and three quarter turns about the centre. Step 3: in Grid B the four L shapes are each a quarter turn round from the next, like a pinwheel. Grid A is mirror images (order 2), Grid C has only two L shapes (order 2), and Grid D's copies are not turned. Answer: Grid B.

misconceptions.0: Grid A copies the L as mirror images in the two lines through the centre. That pattern only fits onto itself after a half turn: order 2. For order 4, each new L must be the L TURNED a quarter turn about the centre.
misconceptions.2: Grid C only adds a half-turn copy, so it fits after 180° and 360°: order 2. Order 4 needs a copy after every quarter turn: four L shapes.
misconceptions.3: Grid D slides copies of the L into the other quarters without turning them. A quarter turn does not fit this pattern onto itself. Turn each copy a quarter turn about the centre.

questions.prompt: Priya says: "Every shape that has rotational symmetry of order 2 or more also has at least one line of symmetry." Look at the shapes. Which shape shows that Priya is wrong?
questions.solution: Step 1: to show a claim is wrong, find a shape where the first part is true but the second part is false: rotational symmetry, but no line of symmetry. Step 2: Shape C (three identical bent arms) fits onto itself after every third of a turn (120°), so it has order 3. Step 3: fold it along any line and the bent arms point the wrong way, so it has no lines of symmetry. Shape C shows Priya is wrong. The triangle and the rectangle have both kinds of symmetry, and the kite has no rotational symmetry.

misconceptions.0: The equilateral triangle has rotational symmetry of order 3 AND 3 lines of symmetry, so it agrees with Priya. To show she is wrong you need a shape with rotational symmetry and NO lines of symmetry.
misconceptions.1: The rectangle has rotational symmetry of order 2 AND 2 lines of symmetry, so it agrees with Priya. Look for a shape that turns onto itself but cannot be folded in half to match.
misconceptions.3: The kite has a line of symmetry but no rotational symmetry (order 1), so it does not test Priya's claim at all. Her claim is about shapes that DO have rotational symmetry.

questions.prompt: Triangle ABC is drawn on the grid. It is rotated 90° clockwise about vertex A. What are the coordinates of the image of B?
questions.solution: Step 1: Trace the shape, pin the tracing down at the centre with your pencil point, and turn the tracing a quarter turn clockwise: an arm from the centre that pointed right now points down, and one that pointed up now points right. Step 2: A(2, 3) stays where it is. The arm AB points 3 squares right of A. Step 3: after a quarter turn clockwise it points 3 squares down from A: (2, 3 - 3) = (2, 0). Check: the arm is still 3 squares long and has turned through 90°.

misconceptions.0: (2, 6) is a quarter turn ANTICLOCKWISE: the arm AB would point up. Clockwise is the way clock hands go, so an arm pointing right turns to point down.
misconceptions.1: (-1, 3) is a half turn (180°): the arm AB would point left. A 90° turn is only a quarter turn, so the arm should point down.
misconceptions.2: (3, -5) is what you get by turning about the origin (0, 0). The centre here is A(2, 3): pin the tracing at A, not at (0, 0).

questions.prompt: Rectangle PQRS is drawn on the grid. It is rotated 90° anticlockwise about vertex P. What are the coordinates of the image of Q?
questions.solution: Step 1: Trace the shape, pin the tracing down at the centre with your pencil point, and turn the tracing a quarter turn anticlockwise: an arm from the centre that pointed right now points up, and one that pointed up now points left. Step 2: P(-2, 1) stays where it is. The arm PQ points 3 squares up from P. Step 3: after a quarter turn anticlockwise it points 3 squares left of P: (-2 - 3, 1) = (-5, 1). Check: the arm is still 3 squares long and has turned through 90°.

misconceptions.1: (1, 1) is a quarter turn CLOCKWISE: the arm PQ would point right. Anticlockwise is against the clock hands, so an arm pointing up turns to point left.
misconceptions.2: (-4, -2) is what you get by turning Q about the origin (0, 0). The centre here is P(-2, 1): pin the tracing at P.
misconceptions.3: (-2, -2) is a half turn (180°): the arm PQ would point down. A 90° turn is only a quarter turn, so the arm should point left.

questions.prompt: Triangle KLM is drawn on the grid. It is rotated 90° clockwise about vertex K. What are the coordinates of the image of M?
questions.solution: Step 1: Trace the shape, pin the tracing down at the centre with your pencil point, and turn the tracing a quarter turn clockwise: an arm from the centre that pointed right now points down, and one that pointed up now points right. Step 2: K(1, 2) stays put. To get from K to M you go 2 right and 3 up. Step 3: turn each move a quarter turn clockwise: 2 right becomes 2 down, and 3 up becomes 3 right. Step 4: from K go 3 right and 2 down: (1 + 3, 2 - 2) = (4, 0). Check: L (3 right of K) goes to 3 down, (1, -1); each side from K keeps its length and turns through 90°.

misconceptions.0: (-2, 4) is a quarter turn ANTICLOCKWISE. Clockwise is the way clock hands go: from K, 'right' turns into 'down' and 'up' turns into 'right'.
misconceptions.2: (-1, 5) is a reflection in the upright line through K: M has been flipped to the left, not turned. In a rotation every arm from K turns through 90°; here the arm KM has not turned through 90°.
misconceptions.3: (5, -3) is what you get by turning M about the origin (0, 0). The centre is K(1, 2): work out the moves from K, not from (0, 0).
misconceptions.4: (-1, -1) is a half turn (180°). A 90° turn is only a quarter turn: 'right' turns into 'down', not into 'left'.

questions.prompt: Triangle ABC is rotated 90° anticlockwise about the marked vertex A. Which grid shows the correct image? The dashed triangle is the image.
questions.solution: Step 1: Trace the shape, pin the tracing down at the centre with your pencil point, and turn the tracing a quarter turn anticlockwise: an arm from the centre that pointed right now points up, and one that pointed up now points left. Step 2: A(3, 3) stays put. Side AB goes 2 squares right, so in the image it goes 2 squares up: (3, 5). Step 3: from A, C is 1 right and 2 up; turned anticlockwise that is 1 up and 2 left: (1, 4). Step 4: the image has corners (3, 3), (3, 5) and (1, 4): Grid D. Check: each side from A keeps its length and has turned through 90°.

misconceptions.0: Grid A shows a quarter turn CLOCKWISE: side AB, which pointed right, now points down. Anticlockwise is against the clock hands, so AB should point up.
misconceptions.1: Grid B shows a half turn (180°): side AB now points left. A 90° turn is only a quarter turn, so AB should point up.
misconceptions.2: Grid C shows a reflection in the horizontal line through A: side AB has not moved at all and the triangle is flipped over. In a rotation every side from A turns through 90°.
